101.quote_or_event: Asked who should receive the rain of treasure that fell when she fed Mahāvīra, the former slave-girl Candanā answered: “Sheth Dhanāvaha, truly my father because of his protection of me.”
101.explanation: In Hemacandra's life of Mahāvīra, the merchant Dhanāvaha buys the captive princess Vasumatī off the street purely out of compassion, though she was a stranger who owed him nothing; when the gods later shower treasure on her, she gives the whole of it to him.
101.tie_back: Dhanāvaha's help came to a girl who had never done anything for him, and Candanā's answer treats that unearned rescue as worth more than a divine treasure, which is the measure Valluvar sets for help given without prior cause.
101.source: Hemacandra, Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra, Book X (Mahāvīracaritra), ch. IV, part 7 'The story of Candanā' (tr. Helen M. Johnson, GOS; wisdomlib.org)
101._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on wisdomlib; a narrative illustration rather than a doctrinal statement, and the Kural's cosmic hyperbole (earth and heaven cannot repay) is only implied by her gift of the treasure.

102.quote_or_event: “Master, even if this food is not suitable, nevertheless, accept it, you who delight only in benefits to others. Favor me.”
102.explanation: Mahāvīra had vowed to accept alms only under very exacting conditions, and kings, ministers and wealthy households failed to feed him for months; the chained Candanā finally offered him a little kulmāṣa (boiled pulse) from the corner of a winnowing basket, and the gods marked the moment with a rain of treasure.
102.tie_back: The humblest possible gift, given at the one moment it was needed, ended a fast of almost six months that all the riches of Kauśāmbī could not, which illustrates Valluvar's point that timeliness makes a small help outweigh the world.
102.source: Hemacandra, Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra, Book X, ch. IV, parts 6-7 'Vīra's special vow' and 'The story of Candanā' (tr. Helen M. Johnson, GOS; wisdomlib.org)
102._accuracy_note: Quote verified on wisdomlib; strong narrative fit on smallness and timing, but the story celebrates the giver's merit more than the recipient's gratitude, and it shares a narrative with the entry for 101.

103.quote_or_event: “They say that in the time of drought the well of spring-water will preserve the inhabitants, though by drawing its water they subsist. So the duty of liberality is found with the great, even when in declining circumstances; with others, even when they are rich, it is rare.”
103.explanation: The Jain-authored Nālaḍiyār pictures true generosity as a spring-fed well that keeps giving in drought without asking anything back.
103.tie_back: Valluvar's benefactor gives without weighing the return, and the Nālaḍiyār's well that sustains the village in drought is the same unreckoning goodness that the recipient should judge greater than the sea.
103.source: Nālaḍiyār ch. 19 'Greatness', st. 4 (= st. 184), English translation in The Indian Antiquary (wisdomlib.org)
103._accuracy_note: A Tamil Jain text, used because no canonical scripture found addresses this closely. It praises the unreckoning giver but says nothing of how the recipient should value the help, so the fit is partial.

104.quote_or_event: “Those who are at the bottom in (the scale of) friendship are like the areca-tree; those others who are in the middle are like the cocoanut-tree. The friendship of those who have experience of the past is like the palmyra-tree, (whose uses are) difficult to reckon.”
104.explanation: The Nālaḍiyār grades friends by trees, placing at the top those who remember the past, whose benefits are as uncountable as the palmyra's.
104.tie_back: Both texts use the palmyra as the image of immeasurable worth, but the Kural's point is that the grateful magnify a millet-sized favour into a palm, while the Nālaḍiyār only ranks friendships by the palm, so the parallel is mainly in the imagery.
104.source: Nālaḍiyār ch. 22 'The choice of friends', st. 6 (= st. 216), English translation in The Indian Antiquary (wisdomlib.org)
104._accuracy_note: Next-best match from a Tamil Jain text: it shares the palmyra image and links lasting friendship to remembering the past, but it lacks the millet-to-palm magnification of a small kindness.

105.explanation: Hemacandra's list of thirty-five qualities of the ideal Jain householder includes kṛtajña, literally 'one who knows what has been done (for him)', alongside being ready to serve others and supporting dependents.
105.tie_back: Jain householder ethics treats gratitude as part of a person's settled character, which matches Valluvar's claim that the worth of a requital depends on the nobility of the one who received the help.
105.source: Hemacandra, Yogaśāstra, list of 35 qualities of the ideal śrāvaka, no. 28, as rendered in Vilas A. Sangave, 'Prescription of Ethical Code' (jainworld.com)
105._accuracy_note: Verified on Sangave's jainworld page (a secondary rendering of Hemacandra's list); it establishes gratitude as a mark of good character but does not make the Kural's specific claim about measuring a favour by the recipient.

106.quote_or_event: “Men cleave not to those to whom their hearts cleave not, within a short space of time; but will the friendship which cherishes the memory of those who are intertwined with one's heart be abandoned, though they are absent from us for a long time?”
106.explanation: The Nālaḍiyār holds that a bond woven into the heart is not given up, however long the separation.
106.tie_back: Valluvar forbids both forgetting the friendship of the stainless and forsaking those who stood by us in distress, and this quatrain likewise insists that a true bond is neither forgotten nor abandoned.
106.source: Nālaḍiyār ch. 22 'The choice of friends', st. 4 (= st. 214), English translation in The Indian Antiquary (wisdomlib.org)
106._accuracy_note: A Tamil Jain text; it matches the 'do not forget, do not forsake' structure but does not specifically name those who helped in adversity.

107.quote_or_event: Prince Pārśva pulled a log from the ascetic Kaṭha's fire and saved the serpent burning inside it; reborn as Dharaṇa, king of the Nāgas, the serpent came when Pārśva was later assailed in meditation, raised him on a lotus, sheltered him with seven hoods, and told the attacker, “I am the servant of the Compassionate.”
107.explanation: In Hemacandra's life of Pārśvanātha, a benefit received in one birth is remembered and repaid in the next, when the rescued serpent, now a Nāga king, shields his rescuer from Meghamālin's flood.
107.tie_back: Valluvar says the good remember, through seven births, those who wiped away their distress, and Jain narrative gives exactly that: gratitude that survives death and rebirth.
107.source: Hemacandra, Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra, Book IX (Pārśvanāthacaritra), ch. III, part 9 'Attacks by Meghamālin' (tr. Helen M. Johnson, GOS; wisdomlib.org)
107._accuracy_note: The quoted line and the episode were verified on wisdomlib; the framing narrative is my summary. It is a close fit, framed within Jain rebirth doctrine rather than a seven-birth count, and the same passage also supplies the entry for 110.

108.quote_or_event: “If a monk hears bad words, cruel and rankling ones, he should silently overlook them, and not take them to heart.”
108.explanation: Among the twenty-two hardships a Jain monk must endure, Mahāvīra lists abuse, which is to be let go of at once rather than nursed as a grievance.
108.tie_back: This matches the second half of the Kural, letting go of a wrong that very day, though the Jain verse does not pair it with the duty to remember a kindness.
108.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 2.25 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45; sacred-texts.com)
108._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; it is a canonical match for forgetting injuries, but it covers only half of the Kural's asymmetric 'remember good, forget harm'.

109.quote_or_event: “Even though they do what is disagreeable, one should preserve as gold those who ought not to be forsaken. Daily do men seek for fire and keep it in their house, though it has consumed both their good house and gold.”
109.explanation: In its chapter on bearing with the faults of others, the Nālaḍiyār teaches that those bound to us by past good are kept, like the household fire, even after they have done us grave harm.
109.tie_back: Valluvar says even a near-mortal injury from a former benefactor fades when one recalls their one good deed, and the Nālaḍiyār likewise lets past worth outweigh present harm.
109.source: Nālaḍiyār ch. 23 'The bearing with the faults of others', st. 5 (= st. 225), English translation in The Indian Antiquary (wisdomlib.org)
109._accuracy_note: A Tamil Jain text. The wisdomlib text has the typo 'consnmed', silently corrected here to 'consumed'. It is a good thematic fit, though the Nālaḍiyār grounds forbearance in friendship rather than explicitly in remembering a past benefit.

110.quote_or_event: “What crime against you was committed by the Lord, when he showed the snake being burned inside the log, if you were prevented from sin at that time? Good advice then led to your hostility, villain, like rain-water on saline soil.”
110.explanation: Kaṭha, reborn as the demon Meghamālin, repays Pārśva's kindly correction with lifelong hostility. Confronted by Dharaṇa, he is terrified: “I can not remain in the three worlds because of the crime against him … Where shall I go for a refuge?”
110.tie_back: Valluvar holds that whoever kills a benefit has no escape, and Hemacandra's ingrate himself finds no refuge anywhere in the three worlds for returning good with harm.
110.source: Hemacandra, Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra, Book IX, ch. III, part 9 'Attacks by Meghamālin' (tr. Helen M. Johnson, GOS; wisdomlib.org)
110._accuracy_note: Both passages were verified verbatim on wisdomlib, and the 'no refuge' closely mirrors the Kural. In the Jain story, however, Meghamālin finds refuge by asking Pārśva's forgiveness, so the Kural's absolute verdict is softened. Same passage as 107.
